newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Vladivostok in fury over power cuts, wage delays.
newsitem.headline: Vladivostok in fury over power cuts, wage delays.

text.p: Hundreds of people including miners and pensioners protested on Friday against wage delays and chronic power cuts in Russia's Far East and called for direct presidential rule in the region.

In the latest sign of rising anger, the demonstrators gathered outside the regional government building in the strategic port city of Vladivostok to demand the resignation of governor Yevgeny Nazdratenko.

"We are left with no choice but to appeal directly to the president. Surely Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin) can see how our region is dying because of our incompetent leadership," said a miner, reading a prepared union statement.
The statement said the miners were pinning their hopes on newly-promoted reformers in the central government, especially Finance Minister Anatoly Chubais.
Like millions of other workers across Russia, the miners have not been paid for many months due to a complex web of debt between producers and consumers, companies and the government.

Earlier this week the miners stopped coal deliveries to local power stations. Their move worsened the already acute energy crisis that led the city authorities last week to declare a state of emergency to ensure electricity supplies to vital services like hospitals.
Many of the demonstrators expressed their anger at the power cuts that have become a regular feature of life in the region. Most held the regional government responsible for the crisis.

"We suffer terribly. It's not just the electricity, we have no hot water and often no cold either. The crisis had been going on for three years but it has got much worse lately," said engineer Vera Ivanova.
In the worst-affected district of Vladivostok, power cuts can last for more than 20 hours a day. Hot showers and baths have become a distant memory for many.
"When you come home from work you just don't know whether you will have light or water," said Sasha Shvedov, an interpreter.
In recent days protesters have blocked the main road out of Vladivostok and the city's kindergartens have closed down temporarily.
Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov briefly visited Vladivostok earlier this week but local newspapers said he carefully avoided planned protests.
"You know, when Kulikov came, they turned on the power again. Suddenly we were able to watch our favorite television serials, do the ironing, all sorts of things," said pensioner Galina Sergeyevna.
"Of course, after he left they turned the power off again," she said with a laugh.

Inside the regional government building the governor's spokeswoman told Reuters that the energy crisis was not the fault of Nazdratenko but was closely linked to Russia's broader economic turmoil in the post-communist era.
"They have bad energy shortages in other regions like Sakhalin and Kamchatka but you only hear about Vladivostok because it is a large, visible city," Natalya Vstovskaya said.
"Our energy problems are being used by some as a political weapon to undermine the governor," she added.
